principle_text: When the persuadee expresses empathy but no clear commitment, avoid unclear or grammatically incorrect statements that may reduce the persuasive impact.
When the persuadee acknowledges the problem and expresses empathy, you should make a clear and direct request for donation to encourage immediate commitment.
When the persuadee has already agreed to donate, avoid repeating the request or specifying amounts without adding new motivational value.
When the persuadee agrees to donate, you should ask for the specific donation amount to confirm their commitment and advance the conversation toward securing the donation.
When the persuadee has agreed to donate, avoid simply acknowledging without reinforcing or deepening their commitment to encourage stronger engagement.
When the persuadee has already agreed to donate, avoid making generic positive statements that do not deepen commitment or encourage explicit confirmation.
When the persuadee responds politely but without clear commitment, avoid vague encouragements that do not specify concrete actions or benefits to increase donation willingness.
When the persuadee responds politely without showing increased commitment, avoid ending with only goodwill statements that do not encourage further engagement or reinforce donation intentions.
When the persuadee acknowledges your donation but questions its adequacy, avoid mentioning specific amounts that may seem insufficient or invite criticism.

When the persuadee expresses limited capacity to donate but willingness to contribute, avoid focusing solely on the amount they have given without encouraging deeper emotional engagement or commitment.

When the persuadee responds politely but non-committally to encouragement about donation amounts, avoid minimizing the value of their current contributions or oversimplifying the impact of small donations.
